papers.abstract: Modern large language models (LLMs) demonstrate exceptional performance on knowledge-intensive tasks, yet the theoretical mechanisms underlying knowledge acquisition (storage and memorization) during pre-training and extraction (retrieval and recall) during inference after fine-tuning remain poorly understood. Although prior theoretical studies have explored these processes through analyses of training dynamics, they overlook critical components essential for a comprehensive theory: (1) the multi-layer perceptron (MLP), empirically identified as the primary module for knowledge storage; (2) out-of-distribution (OOD) adaptivity, which enables LLMs to generalize to unseen scenarios post-pre-training; and (3) next-token prediction, the standard autoregressive objective that encodes knowledge as conditional probabilities. In this work, we introduce, to the best of our knowledge, the first theoretical framework that addresses these limitations by examining the training dynamics of one-layer transformers. Under regularity assumptions, we establish that: (i) transformers attain near-optimal training loss during pre-training, demonstrating effective knowledge acquisition; (ii) given a sufficiently large fine-tuning dataset and appropriate data multiplicity conditions, transformers achieve low generalization error on factual knowledge acquired during pre-training but not revisited in fine-tuning, indicating robust knowledge extraction; and (iii) violation of these conditions leads to elevated generalization error, manifesting as hallucinations. Our analysis encompasses both full fine-tuning and low-rank fine-tuning, yielding insights into the efficacy of practical low-rank adaptation methods. We validate our theoretical findings through experiments on synthetic datasets and the real-world PopQA benchmark, employing GPT-2 and Llama-3.2-1B models.

papers.title: Through a Compressed Lens: Investigating The Impact of Quantization on Factual Knowledge Recall
papers.research_question: How does quantization affect factual knowledge recall (FKR) in large language models?
papers.core_contribution: Quantization typically leads to information loss and degrades factual knowledge recall, especially in smaller models, but BitSandBytes is most effective at preserving FKR and quantization remains a viable compression strategy.
papers.conclusion: Quantization generally leads to information loss and factual knowledge recall degradation, but effects vary by model and technique, and it remains a viable compression strategy.
papers.key_findings:
Quantization typically impairs factual knowledge recall, with more pronounced effects in smaller models within a family.
Models quantized to lower bit precision do not consistently underperform higher-precision versions.
Quantization can occasionally improve factual knowledge recall, possibly due to regularization or noise effects.
BitSandBytes (BITSANDBYTES) quantization best preserves the original model's factual knowledge recall capability.
No observed performance degradation is severe enough to compromise quantization as an effective compression strategy.
papers.limitation:
Experiments are confined to English-language datasets.
Experiments are restricted to Llama3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Qwen2.5-14B due to computational constraints.
The study is limited to post-training quantization techniques and does not include lower-bit quantization (e.g., 1-bit or 2-bit) or weight-activation quantization.
future_direction: Extending experiments to multilingual settings.
Investigating the impact of lower-bit quantization (e.g., 1-bit or 2-bit).
Studying the impact of weight-activation quantization, KV cache compression, or quantization-aware training techniques on factual knowledge recall.
papers.abstract: Quantization methods are widely used to accelerate inference and streamline the deployment of large language models (LLMs). Although quantization's effects on various LLM capabilities have been extensively studied, one critical area remains underexplored: factual knowledge recall (FKR), the process by which LLMs access stored knowledge. To this end, we conduct comprehensive experiments using three common quantization techniques at distinct bit widths, in conjunction with interpretability-driven analyses on two tasks, knowledge memorization and latent multi-hop reasoning. We show that quantization typically results in information loss within LLMs, consequently diminishing their capacity for FKR. This effect is particularly amplified in smaller models within the same architectural families. However, models quantized at reduced bit precision do not consistently exhibit inferior performance and occasionally quantization may even enhance model FKR. We find that BitSandBytes demonstrates highest preservation of the original full-precision model's FKR. Despite variability across models and methods, quantization causes modest performance degradation and remains an effective compression strategy.

papers.title: Balancing Knowledge Updates: Toward Unified Modular Editing in LLMs
papers.research_question: How can knowledge editing in LLMs be improved by jointly updating both MLP and Attention modules, rather than focusing solely on MLP modules?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces IntAttn-Edit, a novel knowledge editing method that jointly updates both MLP and Attention modules using a knowledge balancing strategy, which proportionally allocates update magnitudes based on each module's measured contribution to knowledge storage.
papers.conclusion: IntAttn-Edit addresses the limitation of knowledge residuals in existing methods by jointly editing MLP and Attention modules, leading to more balanced and comprehensive knowledge updates that outperform existing approaches.
papers.key_findings:
Attention modules play a substantial role in factual knowledge storage and retrieval, especially in earlier layers, functioning as key-value associative memory structures.
IntAttn-Edit consistently outperforms existing editing baselines (e.g., ROME, MEMIT, AlphaEdit) on benchmarks like ZsRE and WikiData counterfact, achieving higher edit success and portability.
The proposed knowledge balancing strategy, which dynamically allocates update magnitudes between MLP and Attn modules based on their causal contributions, maintains editing performance within an optimal range.
Updating only a subset of knowledge-storage modules (e.g., only MLP) can leave residual outdated knowledge, which IntAttn-Edit mitigates by jointly editing both modules.
Extensive experiments show IntAttn-Edit delivers superior results across different batch sizes and models while maintaining high locality and fluency.
papers.abstract: Knowledge editing has emerged as an efficient approach for updating factual knowledge in large language models (LLMs). It typically locates knowledge storage modules and then modifies their parameters. However, most existing methods focus on the weights of multilayer perceptron (MLP) modules, which are often identified as the main repositories of factual information. Other components, such as attention (Attn) modules, are often ignored during editing. This imbalance can leave residual outdated knowledge and limit editing effectiveness. We perform comprehensive knowledge localization experiments on advanced LLMs and find that Attn modules play a substantial role in factual knowledge storage and retrieval, especially in earlier layers. Based on these insights, we propose IntAttn-Edit, a method that extends the associative memory paradigm to jointly update both MLP and Attn modules. Our approach uses a knowledge balancing strategy that allocates update magnitudes in proportion to each module's measured contribution to knowledge storage. Experiments on standard benchmarks show that IntAttn-Edit achieves higher edit success, better generalization, and stronger knowledge preservation than prior methods. Further analysis shows that the balancing strategy keeps editing performance within an optimal range across diverse settings.

papers.title: Precise Localization of Memories: A Fine-grained Neuron-level Knowledge Editing Technique for LLMs
papers.research_question: How can we improve the locality of knowledge editing in LLMs by moving from causal tracing to neuron-level localization?
papers.core_contribution: FiNE is a neuron-level knowledge editing method that improves editing locality by precisely identifying and modifying neurons in FFNs, overcoming the over-reliance on subject entities in previous causal tracing methods.
papers.conclusion: FiNE advances knowledge localization and editing in LLMs by providing a neuron-level approach that improves locality and efficiency, paving the way for more reliable knowledge management.
papers.key_findings:
Existing locate-then-edit methods based on causal tracing are overly subject-driven and neglect relations, leading to poor editing locality.
FiNE's neuron-level localization provides more precise knowledge localization than causal tracing.
FiNE achieves better locality scores and efficiency compared to existing methods like ROME, MEMIT, and PMET.
FiNE maintains high edit success and portability while significantly improving locality.
Ablation studies show that neuron localization and layer freezing are important components of FiNE.
papers.limitation: The safety of edits cannot be ensured, and there is potential for misuse such as introducing malicious misinformation or bias.
papers.abstract: Knowledge editing aims to update outdated information in Large Language Models (LLMs). A representative line of study is locate-then-edit methods, which typically employ causal tracing to identify the modules responsible for recalling factual knowledge about entities. However, we find these methods are often sensitive only to changes in the subject entity, leaving them less effective at adapting to changes in relations. This limitation results in poor editing locality, which can lead to the persistence of irrelevant or inaccurate facts, ultimately compromising the reliability of LLMs. We believe this issue arises from the insufficient precision of knowledge localization. To address this, we propose a Fine-grained Neuron-level Knowledge Editing (FiNE) method that enhances editing locality without affecting overall success rates. By precisely identifying and modifying specific neurons within feed-forward networks, FiNE significantly improves knowledge localization and editing. Quantitative experiments demonstrate that FiNE efficiently achieves better overall performance compared to existing techniques, providing new insights into the localization and modification of knowledge within LLMs.

papers.title: The Mechanics of Conceptual Interpretation in GPT Models: Interpretative Insights
papers.research_question: What are the observable representation patterns that characterise conceptual interpretation within language models? Can we localise specialised representational patterns to derive an interpretation model within language models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces concept editing, a variation of knowledge editing, to uncover conceptualization mechanisms in LLMs, and through analysis of MLP, MHA, and hidden states, reveals distinct patterns of semantic processing.
papers.conclusion: The work elucidates how transformer models process semantic information through distinct component interactions, paving the way for targeted interventions and improved interpretability techniques.
papers.key_findings:
MLP layers employ key-value retrieval and context-dependent processing, focusing on specific lexical and semantic features.
MHA layers show distributed nature with higher-level activations, suggesting sophisticated semantic integration.
Hidden states emphasize the importance of the last token and top layers in the inference process, indicating gradual information building.
Concept interpretation involves a collaborative process among model components, with compositionality being critical.
Patterns are consistent across languages (English and Spanish) and across alternative definitions, indicating robust processing strategies.
papers.abstract: Locating and editing knowledge in large language models (LLMs) is crucial for enhancing their accuracy, safety, and inference rationale. We introduce ``concept editing'', an innovative variation of knowledge editing that uncovers conceptualisation mechanisms within these models. Using the reverse dictionary task, inference tracing, and input abstraction, we analyse the Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP), Multi-Head Attention (MHA), and hidden state components of transformer models. Our results reveal distinct patterns: MLP layers employ key-value retrieval mechanism and context-dependent processing, which are highly associated with relative input tokens. MHA layers demonstrate a distributed nature with significant higher-level activations, suggesting sophisticated semantic integration. Hidden states emphasise the importance of the last token and top layers in the inference process. We observe evidence of gradual information building and distributed representation. These observations elucidate how transformer models process semantic information, paving the way for targeted interventions and improved interpretability techniques. Our work highlights the complex, layered nature of semantic processing in LLMs and the challenges of isolating and modifying specific concepts within these models.

papers.title: Too Late to Recall: Explaining the Two-Hop Problem in Multimodal Knowledge Retrieval
papers.research_question: Why do many vision language models (VLMs) exhibit reduced factual recall performance compared to their large language model (LLM) backbones, and what is the underlying mechanism?
papers.core_contribution: VLMs suffer from a 'two-hop problem' where entity representations from visual inputs emerge too late in the forward pass, bypassing the early-layer MLP circuits in the LLM backbone responsible for factual recall, leading to performance degradation.
papers.conclusion: The speed of early entity resolution critically determines how effective VLMs are in using preexisting LLM mechanisms; representation misalignment limits VLMs' ability to reuse existing task circuits.
papers.key_findings:
11 out of 14 benchmarked VLMs exhibit factual recall degradation compared to their LLM backbones.
Attribution patching shows degraded VLMs do not use the same early-layer MLPs as their LLM backbones for factual recall.
Activation patching of early-layer MLP outputs from the LLM into the VLM recovers performance, indicating these components are causally crucial.
Linear probing reveals entity representations emerge in middle-to-late layers in degraded VLMs, but early in high-performing VLMs.
Chain-of-thought prompting can mitigate the performance gap for some VLMs, especially larger ones.
papers.limitation: The study focuses on factual recall and may not generalize to other tasks.
future_direction: Investigate better, more data-efficient adapter mechanisms and multimodal alignment techniques.
Examine other tasks beyond factual recall, comparing VLMs against their LLM backbone.
papers.abstract: Training vision language models (VLMs) aims to align visual representations from a vision encoder with the textual representations of a pretrained large language model (LLM). However, many VLMs exhibit reduced factual recall performance compared to their LLM backbones, raising the question of how effective multimodal fine-tuning is at extending existing mechanisms within the LLM to visual inputs. We argue that factual recall based on visual inputs requires VLMs to solve a two-hop problem: (1) forming entity representations from visual inputs, and (2) recalling associated factual knowledge based on these entity representations. By benchmarking 14 VLMs with various architectures (LLaVA, Native, Cross-Attention), sizes (7B-124B parameters), and training setups on factual recall tasks against their original LLM backbone models, we find that 11 of 14 models exhibit factual recall degradation. We select three models with high and two models with low performance degradation, and use attribution patching, activation patching, and probing to show that degraded VLMs struggle to use the existing factual recall circuit of their LLM backbone, because they resolve the first hop too late in the computation. In contrast, high-performing VLMs resolve entity representations early enough to reuse the existing factual recall mechanism. Finally, we demonstrate two methods to recover performance: patching entity representations from the LLM backbone into the VLM, and prompting with chain-of-thought reasoning. Our results highlight that the speed of early entity resolution critically determines how effective VLMs are in using preexisting LLM mechanisms. More broadly, our work illustrates how mechanistic analysis can explain and unveil systematic failures in multimodal alignment.

papers.title: Are Pretrained Language Models Symbolic Reasoners over Knowledge?
papers.research_question: How do pretrained language models learn factual knowledge? Specifically, can they perform symbolic reasoning to infer unseen facts, and what factors affect memorization of facts?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that PLMs can learn some one-hop symbolic reasoning rules but overgeneralize, struggle with two-hop reasoning, and that memorization is influenced by frequency and schema conformity.
papers.conclusion: The study shows that BERT can to some extent infer facts not explicitly seen during training via symbolic rules, and effective knowledge acquisition combines memorization and symbolic reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
BERT can learn one-hop rules like equivalence and implication, but overgeneralizes symmetry and inversion.
BERT struggles with two-hop reasoning (composition) unless provided with richer semantic context (schema).
BERT does not learn a general concept of negation; it relies on co-occurrences.
Memorization is successful for frequent facts and schema-conformant facts; exceptions are harder to memorize unless repeated.
When memory capacity is limited, schema-conformant facts and exceptions compete based on frequency.
papers.limitation:
Variation in generated data is more limited than in naturally occurring data.
Semantics are deliberately restricted to one rule only per generated corpus.
We do not investigate effects of model and corpus size.
future_direction: Relax the simplifying assumptions made in the study.
Improve PLMs' ability to learn symbolic rules by imposing additional inductive biases on architectures or modifying training corpora.
papers.abstract: How can pretrained language models (PLMs) learn factual knowledge from the training set? We investigate the two most important mechanisms: reasoning and memorization. Prior work has attempted to quantify the number of facts PLMs learn, but we present, using synthetic data, the first study that investigates the causal relation between facts present in training and facts learned by the PLM. For reasoning, we show that PLMs seem to learn to apply some symbolic reasoning rules correctly but struggle with others, including two-hop reasoning. Further analysis suggests that even the application of learned reasoning rules is flawed. For memorization, we identify schema conformity (facts systematically supported by other facts) and frequency as key factors for its success.

papers.title: One Mind, Many Tongues: A Deep Dive into Language-Agnostic Knowledge Neurons in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we accurately localize language-agnostic knowledge neurons in large language models, considering uncertainty across queries and languages?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces MATRICE, a method for localizing language-agnostic knowledge neurons by quantifying uncertainty across queries and languages, and constructs the RML-LAMA benchmark. It demonstrates these neurons' roles in cross-lingual editing, knowledge enhancement, and injection.
papers.conclusion: The proposed MATRICE method accurately localizes language-agnostic knowledge neurons, and these neurons are shown to be conducive to cross-lingual knowledge editing, enhancement, and injection.
papers.key_findings:
A significant proportion of language-agnostic knowledge neurons are distributed in the last few layers of LLMs.
Manipulating (suppressing/enhancing) language-agnostic knowledge neurons significantly affects knowledge expression across languages.
A single edit on language-agnostic knowledge neurons can simultaneously modify corresponding knowledge in all languages (cross-lingual editing).
Amplifying the activation of language-agnostic knowledge neurons improves prediction performance in low-resource languages.
Fine-tuning only parameters associated with language-agnostic knowledge neurons helps LLMs learn new knowledge while alleviating forgetting of old knowledge.
papers.limitation: The approach is based on knowledge neuron theory and focuses on factual knowledge, not yet extended to other types like commonsense or event knowledge.
future_direction: Extend the approach to investigate other types of knowledge, such as commonsense knowledge and event knowledge.
Adapt the method to new theoretical frameworks as the theory of knowledge neurons evolves.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have learned vast amounts of factual knowledge through self-supervised pre-training on large-scale corpora. Meanwhile, LLMs have also demonstrated excellent multilingual capabilities, which can express the learned knowledge in multiple languages. However, the knowledge storage mechanism in LLMs still remains mysterious. Some researchers attempt to demystify the factual knowledge in LLMs from the perspective of knowledge neurons, and subsequently discover language-agnostic knowledge neurons that store factual knowledge in a form that transcends language barriers. However, the preliminary finding suffers from two limitations: 1) High Uncertainty in Localization Results. Existing study only uses a prompt-based probe to localize knowledge neurons for each fact, while LLMs cannot provide consistent answers for semantically equivalent queries. Thus, it leads to inaccurate localization results with high uncertainty. 2) Lack of Analysis in More Languages. The study only analyzes language-agnostic knowledge neurons on English and Chinese data, without exploring more language families and languages. Naturally, it limits the generalizability of the findings. To address aforementioned problems, we first construct a new benchmark called Rephrased Multilingual LAMA (RML-LAMA), which contains high-quality cloze-style multilingual parallel queries for each fact. Then, we propose a novel method named Multilingual Integrated Gradients with Uncertainty Estimation (MATRICE), which quantifies the uncertainty across queries and languages during knowledge localization. Extensive experiments show that our method can accurately localize language-agnostic knowledge neurons. We also further investigate the role of language-agnostic knowledge neurons in cross-lingual knowledge editing, knowledge enhancement and new knowledge injection.

papers.title: Editing Conceptual Knowledge for Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Whether LLMs possess the capability to modify concepts (conceptual knowledge) and how to evaluate such modifications.
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces the task of conceptual knowledge editing for LLMs, constructs a benchmark dataset ConceptEdit, and establishes a suite of evaluation metrics including Instance Change and Concept Consistency.
papers.conclusion: Concept editing is a challenging task for LLMs, and existing editing methods have limitations in modifying conceptual knowledge without distorting related instances. This work provides a benchmark and metrics to inspire further research.
papers.key_findings:
Existing knowledge editing methods (FT, ROME, MEMIT, PROMPT) can achieve high reliability in modifying concept-level definitions in LLMs.
These methods perform poorly on concept-specific metrics like Instance Change and Concept Consistency, indicating they distort related instance knowledge.
There is a gap between reliability (token-level accuracy) and concept consistency (semantic similarity of generated definitions).
Concept editing is easier when the replacement definition comes from the same superclass (intra module) compared to a different superclass (inter module).
Causal tracing reveals that conceptual knowledge is stored differently from instance knowledge, with attention mechanisms in earlier layers playing a key role.
papers.limitation:
The experiments are limited to models up to 7B parameters; larger models may exhibit different behaviors.
The generalization of edited concepts to unseen instances or related concepts is not fully explored.
The mechanisms of how LLMs learn and represent concepts and concept hierarchies are not fully understood.
future_direction: Exploring concept editing in larger-scale language models.
Improving the generalization of edited concepts to related knowledge.
Studying the mechanisms of concept learning and representation in LLMs.

papers.title: The Geometry of Truth: Emergent Linear Structure in Large Language Model Representations of True/False Datasets
papers.research_question: Do large language models (LLMs) linearly represent the truth or falsehood of factual statements in their internal representations?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides evidence that at sufficient scale, LLMs compute and linearly represent the truth of factual statements in their internal activations, and introduces mass-mean probing as a simple method that identifies directions more causally implicated in model outputs.
papers.conclusion: The work finds evidence that LLMs linearly represent truth at scale, localizes these representations to specific hidden states, and shows that mass-mean probing is an effective method for identifying causally implicated truth directions.
papers.key_findings:
Linear representations of truth emerge with model scale, with larger models developing a more abstract notion of truth applicable across diverse inputs.
Truth representations are localized to a small group of hidden states (over the end-of-sentence punctuation token) in the residual stream.
Simple difference-in-mean (mass-mean) probes generalize as well as other probing techniques (logistic regression, CCS) for larger models and identify directions that are more causally effective in intervention experiments.
Training probes on datasets that include statements and their logical opposites (e.g., cities and neg cities) improves generalization, mitigating the effect of non-truth correlated features.
Probes trained solely on text likelihood (the likely dataset) perform poorly on datasets where truth and probability are anti-correlated, indicating the represented feature is not merely text probability.
papers.limitation:
Focuses on simple, uncontroversial factual statements, so cannot disambiguate truth from closely related features like 'commonly believed' or 'verifiable'.
Studies only models in the LLaMA-2 family, so results may not generalize to all LLMs.
future_direction: Why were interventions with mass-mean probe directions extracted from the likely dataset effective, despite these probes being inaccurate at classification?
Why did mass-mean probing with the cities+neg_cities training data perform poorly for the 70B model, while mass-mean probing with larger_than+smaller_than performed well?
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have impressive capabilities, but are prone to outputting falsehoods. Recent work has developed techniques for inferring whether a LLM is telling the truth by training probes on the LLM's internal activations. However, this line of work is controversial, with some authors pointing out failures of these probes to generalize in basic ways, among other conceptual issues. In this work, we use high-quality datasets of simple true/false statements to study in detail the structure of LLM representations of truth, drawing on three lines of evidence: 1. Visualizations of LLM true/false statement representations, which reveal clear linear structure. 2. Transfer experiments in which probes trained on one dataset generalize to different datasets. 3. Causal evidence obtained by surgically intervening in a LLM's forward pass, causing it to treat false statements as true and vice versa. Overall, we present evidence that at sufficient scale, LLMs linearly represent the truth or falsehood of factual statements. We also show that simple difference-in-mean probes generalize as well as other probing techniques while identifying directions which are more causally implicated in model outputs.

papers.title: Rigorously Assessing Natural Language Explanations of Neurons
papers.research_question: How can we rigorously evaluate the faithfulness of natural language explanations that claim individual neurons in a language model represent a concept?
papers.core_contribution: The paper develops a framework with observational and intervention modes to evaluate natural language explanations of neurons, and applies it to show that GPT-4-generated explanations for GPT-2 XL neurons have low faithfulness and causal efficacy.
papers.conclusion: Natural language may not be the best medium for model explanations due to vagueness and ambiguity, and neurons may not be the optimal unit of analysis; structured formalisms and analysis of neuron groups are promising alternatives.
papers.key_findings:
Even among the top 0.6% of neurons with GPT-4 explanation scores ≥0.8, explanations achieve only 0.64 precision and 0.50 recall.
Intervention-based evaluation shows GPT-4 explanations have little to no causal efficacy, performing similarly to random baselines.
Individual neurons are not effective causal mediators; causal effects require aggregating over many neurons, especially in early MLP layers.
Natural language explanations are often vague and ambiguous, making them unreliable for technical decision-making.
The GPT-4 score used by Bills et al. (2023) is insensitive to Type I errors and does not guarantee faithful explanations.
papers.limitation:
Analysis is primarily on GPT-2 XL; results may not extend directly to other architectures.
Faithful explanations could be used for malicious manipulations of models.
future_direction: Use structured formalisms (e.g., programming languages) instead of natural language for explanations.
Analyze groups of neurons or other network components (e.g., attention heads, residual streams) as units of analysis.
Conduct similar evaluations on other model architectures.
papers.abstract: Natural language is an appealing medium for explaining how large language models process and store information, but evaluating the faithfulness of such explanations is challenging. To help address this, we develop two modes of evaluation for natural language explanations that claim individual neurons represent a concept in a text input. In the *observational mode*, we evaluate claims that a neuron a activates on all and only input strings that refer to a concept picked out by the proposed explanation E. In the *intervention mode*, we construe E as a claim that neuron a is a causal mediator of the concept denoted by E. We apply our framework to the GPT-4-generated explanations of GPT-2 XL neurons of Bills et al. (2023) and show that even the most confident explanations have high error rates and little to no causal efficacy. We close the paper by critically assessing whether natural language is a good choice for explanations and whether neurons are the best level of analysis.

papers.title: Tracing and Dissecting How LLMs Recall Factual Knowledge for Real World Questions
papers.research_question: How do large language models (LLMs) internally reason and recall factual knowledge when generating multi-token rationales for real-world commonsense question answering?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces an interpretability framework that reveals a consistent three-phase pattern (Subject Augmentation and Broadcasting, Object Retrieval and Reranking, Conclusion Fusion and Generation) in LLMs' factual knowledge recall, and uses these insights to improve model performance via selective fine-tuning.
papers.conclusion: The proposed two-dimensional interpretability framework effectively uncovers the internal reasoning process of LLMs in factual knowledge recall, and the insights gained can be directly applied to improve model performance through targeted interventions like selective fine-tuning.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs follow a three-phase pattern during commonsense reasoning: Subject Augmentation and Broadcasting, Object Retrieval and Reranking, and Conclusion Fusion and Generation.
Attention heads are responsible for retrieving and fusing relevant object information, while MLPs rerank and select the most appropriate object for output.
LLMs often fail not due to a lack of knowledge, but because they struggle to select the most accurate fact during the retrieval and rerank phase based on contextual cues.
Selective fine-tuning of key attention heads and MLPs identified through interpretability analysis significantly improves model accuracy on both in-domain and out-of-domain tasks.
Reasoning conjunctive adverbs (e.g., 'Thus') serve as anchors for gathering and transferring conclusion-related information in the reasoning process.
papers.abstract: Yiqun Wang, Chaoqun Wan, Sile Hu, Yonggang Zhang, Xiang Tian, Yaowu Chen, Xu Shen, Jieping Ye. Proceedings of the 63rd Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1: Long Papers). 2025.

papers.title: Large Scale Knowledge Washing
papers.research_question: How to unlearn a large amount of factual knowledge from large language models while minimizing the effects on the model's reasoning ability?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes LAW, a method for large-scale knowledge washing that updates MLP layers in LLMs to forget factual knowledge while preserving reasoning ability.
papers.conclusion: LAW is an effective method for large-scale knowledge washing, successfully removing target knowledge while maintaining reasoning ability and model fluency.
papers.key_findings:
LAW achieves more thorough knowledge washing (lower accuracy on target facts) compared to existing methods like MEMIT, FT, etc.
LAW maintains the model's reasoning ability and fluency, as shown by performance on reasoning benchmarks and perplexity.
LAW is effective at large scale (e.g., 332,036 facts) without destroying the model.
LAW preserves unrelated knowledge similarly to MEMIT.
The method is model-agnostic and works for transformer-based models with MLP layers.
papers.limitation:
The method currently only works on GPT-2 and GPT-J due to implementation constraints with MEMIT for other models like LLaMA.
After unlearning, the model may generate arbitrary answers, which could lead to hallucination, though this can be mitigated by instruction tuning.
future_direction: Extend the method to other models like LLaMA.
Use instruction tuning to regulate the model's response behavior after unlearning.
papers.abstract: Large language models show impressive abilities in memorizing world knowledge, which leads to concerns regarding memorization of private information, toxic or sensitive knowledge, and copyrighted content. We introduce the problem of Large Scale Knowledge Washing, focusing on unlearning an extensive amount of factual knowledge. Previous unlearning methods usually define the reverse loss and update the model via backpropagation, which may affect the model's fluency and reasoning ability or even destroy the model due to extensive training with the reverse loss. Existing works introduce additional data from downstream tasks to prevent the model from losing capabilities, which requires downstream task awareness. Controlling the tradeoff of unlearning and maintaining existing capabilities is also challenging. To this end, we propose LAW (Large Scale Washing) to update the MLP layers in decoder-only large language models to perform knowledge washing, as inspired by model editing methods and based on the hypothesis that knowledge and reasoning are disentanglable. We derive a new objective with the knowledge to be unlearned to update the weights of certain MLP layers. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of LAW in forgetting target knowledge while maintaining reasoning ability. The code will be open-sourced at https://github.com/wangyu-ustc/LargeScaleWashing.

papers.title: Distributional Associations vs In-Context Reasoning: A Study of Feed-forward and Attention Layers
papers.research_question: What is the distinction between feed-forward and attention layers in transformers regarding distributional associations and in-context reasoning?
papers.core_contribution: Feed-forward layers in transformers learn distributional associations (e.g., bigrams) early in training, while attention layers learn in-context reasoning; truncating feed-forward layers can improve reasoning performance by removing distributional biases.
papers.conclusion: Distributional associations and in-context reasoning mechanisms are learned during training and tend to be disentangled in different parts of the model, such that selectively removing feed-forward components can lead to better predictions in reasoning tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Feed-forward layers quickly learn distributional associations (e.g., trigger-noise association) in early training steps.
Attention layers learn to attend to in-context targets and avoid noise tokens.
In models without feed-forward layers, the noise association is stored in a low-rank subspace of the value matrix.
Truncating feed-forward layers (e.g., via LASER) in pre-trained models improves performance on reasoning tasks by reducing distributional biases.
Theoretical analysis shows that gradients for feed-forward layers are less noisy and thus learn distributional associations faster.
papers.abstract: Large language models have been successful at tasks involving basic forms of in-context reasoning, such as generating coherent language, as well as storing vast amounts of knowledge. At the core of the Transformer architecture behind such models are feed-forward and attention layers, which are often associated to knowledge and reasoning, respectively. In this paper, we study this distinction empirically and theoretically in a controlled synthetic setting where certain next-token predictions involve both distributional and in-context information. We find that feed-forward layers tend to learn simple distributional associations such as bigrams, while attention layers focus on in-context reasoning. Our theoretical analysis identifies the noise in the gradients as a key factor behind this discrepancy. Finally, we illustrate how similar disparities emerge in pre-trained models through ablations on the Pythia model family on simple reasoning tasks.

papers.title: Cutting Off the Head Ends the Conflict: A Mechanism for Interpreting and Mitigating Knowledge Conflicts in Language Models
papers.research_question: What is the mechanism of knowledge conflicts in language models, and how can they be mitigated by precise interventions at the pivotal point?
papers.core_contribution: The paper reveals that knowledge conflicts in language models arise from the integration of inconsistent information flows by memory heads and context heads in later layers, and proposes a parameter-free method (PH3) to mitigate conflicts by pruning these heads.
papers.conclusion: The paper provides a mechanistic interpretation of knowledge conflicts in LMs and demonstrates that the proposed PH3 method can effectively mitigate these conflicts and control model behavior, showing strong generalization across models, relations, and data formats.
papers.key_findings:
FFNs in early layers enrich the semantic information of input elements, while MHAs in middle and late layers are crucial for passing information to the last token.
The last token extracts attribute information from the context subject (internal memory) and context attribute (external context) in later layers.
Some attention heads in late MHAs play opposite roles: memory heads recall knowledge from internal memory, and context heads retrieve knowledge from external context.
The pivotal point of knowledge conflict is the integration of inconsistent information flows by memory heads and context heads.
The proposed PH3 method can flexibly control LMs to use internal memory (↑44.0%) or external context (↑38.5%) by pruning conflicting attention heads without updating parameters.

papers.title: On the Generalizability of "Competition of Mechanisms: Tracing How Language Models Handle Facts and Counterfactuals"
papers.research_question: Does the competition of mechanisms between factual recall and counterfactual repetition, as identified by Ortu et al. (2024), generalize to larger models, different prompt structures, and across domains?
papers.core_contribution: The attention head ablation method from Ortu et al. (2024) does not generalize well; its effectiveness varies significantly with model architecture, prompt structure, and domain.
papers.conclusion: The competition of mechanisms identified by Ortu et al. (2024) is not fully generalizable; experimental findings in mechanistic interpretability are highly dependent on the specific model, prompt structure, and domain.
papers.key_findings:
Successfully reproduced the original findings on GPT-2 small and Pythia 6.9B regarding positional information encoding, attention block dominance, and attention head specialization.
In Llama 3.1 8B, attention head specialization is greatly reduced, and the logit lens method shows limited early-layer activity and a sharp final-layer activation.
Changing the prompt structure to a question-answering format reduces the model's propensity to repeat the counterfactual, indicating sensitivity to repetition.
The choice of premise word (e.g., 'Redefine', 'Validate') affects the rate of factual vs. counterfactual predictions and the effectiveness of attention head ablation.
The effectiveness of the proposed attention head ablation varies across domains; it works best for domains where the factual token is leaked in the subject (e.g., 'Autos and Vehicles') and fails for others.
papers.limitation:
The logit lens method may be unreliable for larger models like Llama 3.1 8B, potentially failing to capture early-layer mechanisms.
The filtered MQuAKE dataset used for domain analysis is very small (228 prompts), limiting definitive conclusions.
Most extended findings rely on GPT-2 small and a dataset derived from Ortu et al. (2024), limiting generalizability to other models and datasets.
future_direction: Investigate whether larger models distribute work more evenly across heads or if newer interpretability techniques (e.g., circuit analysis, tuned lens) are needed to capture their mechanisms.
Conduct a deeper analysis of why certain dataset domains impact attention head activation, distinguishing between token leakage, topic words, and task difficulty.
Extend the findings to different, larger datasets and models, as well as new prompt structures and premise words.
papers.abstract: We present a reproduction study of "Competition of Mechanisms: Tracing How Language Models Handle Facts and Counterfactuals" (Ortu et al., 2024), which investigates competition of mechanisms in language models between factual recall and counterfactual in-context repetition. Our study successfully reproduces their primary findings regarding the localization of factual and counterfactual information, the dominance of attention blocks in mechanism competition, and the specialization of attention heads in handling competing information. We reproduce their results on both GPT-2 (Radford et al., 2019) and Pythia 6.9B (Biderman et al., 2023). We extend their work in three significant directions. First, we explore the generalizability of these findings to even larger models by replicating the experiments on Llama 3.1 8B (Grattafiori et al., 2024), discovering greatly reduced attention head specialization. Second, we investigate the impact of prompt structure by introducing variations where we avoid repeating the counterfactual statement verbatim or we change the premise word, observing a marked decrease in the logit for the counterfactual token. Finally, we test the validity of the authors' claims for prompts of specific domains, discovering that certain categories of prompts skew the results by providing the factual prediction token as part of the subject of the sentence. Overall, we find that the attention head ablation proposed in Ortu et al. (2024) is ineffective for domains that are underrepresented in their dataset, and that the effectiveness varies based on model architecture, prompt structure, domain and task.

papers.title: Towards Tracing Factual Knowledge in Language Models Back to the Training Data
papers.research_question: How can we identify which training examples taught a language model to generate a particular factual assertion?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the fact tracing problem and the first quantitative benchmark for evaluating training data attribution methods, showing that current methods underperform simple IR baselines and have significant room for improvement.
papers.conclusion: Current TDA methods have limitations in fact tracing, with BM25 outperforming them on real data, and key challenges like gradient saturation need to be addressed for future improvement.
papers.key_findings:
BM25 outperforms gradient-based and embedding-based TDA methods on the FTRACE-TREX dataset with real facts.
On the synthetic FTRACE-SYNTH dataset, TDA methods perform better, especially when lexical overlap is reduced.
Gradient normalization and the use of Adafactor accumulators significantly improve TracIn performance.
The embedding layer provides the most reliable attribution signal for both gradient and embedding-based methods.
There is substantial headroom for improving TDA methods for fact tracing, as they do not yet reliably outperform model-agnostic baselines.
papers.limitation:
Gradient saturation can cause TDA methods to fail when the model's loss is already zero at the start of the training period monitored.
Lexical overlap between queries and training examples can confound attribution methods, favoring simple IR baselines.
future_direction: Overcoming the problem of gradient saturation
Improving TDA methods to handle lexical variation in fact expression
Developing more accurate and scalable fact tracing techniques
papers.abstract: Language models (LMs) have been shown to memorize a great deal of factual knowledge contained in their training data. But when an LM generates an assertion, it is often difficult to determine where it learned this information and whether it is true. In this paper, we propose the problem of fact tracing: identifying which training examples taught an LM to generate a particular factual assertion. Prior work on training data attribution (TDA) may offer effective tools for identifying such examples, known as "proponents". We present the first quantitative benchmark to evaluate this. We compare two popular families of TDA methods -- gradient-based and embedding-based -- and find that much headroom remains. For example, both methods have lower proponent-retrieval precision than an information retrieval baseline (BM25) that does not have access to the LM at all. We identify key challenges that may be necessary for further improvement such as overcoming the problem of gradient saturation, and also show how several nuanced implementation details of existing neural TDA methods can significantly improve overall fact tracing performance.

papers.title: Have Faith in Faithfulness: Going Beyond Circuit Overlap When Finding Model Mechanisms
papers.research_question: How faithful are circuits found by edge attribution patching (EAP), and what is the relationship between overlap and faithfulness? The paper also introduces a new method, EAP-IG, to improve faithfulness.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces EAP-IG, a gradient-based circuit finding method that produces more faithful circuits than EAP, and shows that overlap metrics are insufficient for evaluating circuit faithfulness.
papers.conclusion: When comparing circuits, measuring overlap is no substitute for measuring faithfulness; EAP-IG provides a more faithful alternative to EAP for circuit finding.
papers.key_findings:
EAP-IG circuits are more faithful than EAP circuits on many tasks, though activation patching circuits sometimes outperform both.
Overlap (node or edge) does not always imply faithfulness; moderate overlap does not predict faithfulness well.
EAP-IG scores have higher correlation with activation patching scores for important edges, leading to more faithful circuits.
EAP-IG requires few steps (e.g., m=5) to achieve high faithfulness, making it efficient.
Cross-task faithfulness analysis reveals that circuit mechanisms can be shared across related tasks (e.g., Greater-Than variants) but not always.
papers.limitation:
Testing circuit completeness is challenging, and manually-found 'ground-truth' circuits may be unreliable.
EAP-IG does not always match the performance of activation patching (e.g., on the IOI task).
future_direction: Developing more efficient algorithms for computing faithfulness.
Investigating weighted graph edit distance as a metric that accounts for edge importance.
Exploring methods to ensure circuit completeness in addition to faithfulness.
papers.abstract: Many recent language model (LM) interpretability studies have adopted the circuits framework, which aims to find the minimal computational subgraph, or circuit, that explains LM behavior on a given task. Most studies determine which edges belong in a LM's circuit by performing causal interventions on each edge independently, but this scales poorly with model size. Edge attribution patching (EAP), gradient-based approximation to interventions, has emerged as a scalable but imperfect solution to this problem. In this paper, we introduce a new method - EAP with integrated gradients (EAP-IG) - that aims to better maintain a core property of circuits: faithfulness. A circuit is faithful if all model edges outside the circuit can be ablated without changing the model's performance on the task; faithfulness is what justifies studying circuits, rather than the full model. Our experiments demonstrate that circuits found using EAP are less faithful than those found using EAP-IG, even though both have high node overlap with circuits found previously using causal interventions. We conclude more generally that when using circuits to compare the mechanisms models use to solve tasks, faithfulness, not overlap, is what should be measured.

papers.title: Benchmarking and Understanding Compositional Relational Reasoning of LLMs
papers.research_question: What is the capability of existing transformer large language models (LLMs) in solving compositional relational reasoning (CRR) tasks, and what are the underlying mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes the Generalized Associative Recall (GAR) benchmark for evaluating compositional relational reasoning in LLMs, revealing their deficiency, and discovers core circuits and True/False attention heads that are fundamental for CRR.
papers.conclusion: The GAR benchmark is challenging for mainstream LLMs and reveals a fundamental deficiency in compositional relational reasoning. Mechanistic interpretability analysis discovers reusable core circuits and identifies True/False attention heads that play fundamental roles in CRR across models and tasks.
papers.key_findings:
GAR is challenging for existing LLMs, with performance dropping significantly for harder tasks and the compositionality gap increasing with model scale.
Attribution patching reveals core circuits reused by Vicuna-33B across different GAR tasks, including a truthfulness sub-circuit and an in-context learning sub-circuit.
Intervention experiments show that correct functioning of identified vital attention heads (e.g., predicting, pre-predicting, higher-order local, induction, and relating heads) significantly impacts task performance.
Two classes of higher-order relating heads (True and False heads) are identified whose activations represent the abstract notion of true and false in GAR tasks.
The activation patterns of the True/False heads generalize to other datasets (SNLI and GoT), indicating they encode information for truthfulness classification beyond GAR.
papers.limitation: The circuit discovery is done manually without using automatic circuit discovery methods, which is left for future work.
future_direction: Automatic circuit discovery methods for larger models and more complex circuits.
papers.abstract: Compositional relational reasoning (CRR) is a hallmark of human intelligence, but we lack a clear understanding of whether and how existing transformer large language models (LLMs) can solve CRR tasks. To enable systematic exploration of the CRR capability of LLMs, we first propose a new synthetic benchmark called Generalized Associative Recall (GAR) by integrating and generalizing the essence of several tasks in mechanistic interpretability (MI) study in a unified framework. Evaluation shows that GAR is challenging enough for existing LLMs, revealing their fundamental deficiency in CRR. Meanwhile, it is easy enough for systematic MI study. Then, to understand how LLMs solve GAR tasks, we use attribution patching to discover the core circuits reused by Vicuna-33B across different tasks, and a set of vital attention heads. Intervention experiments show that the correct functioning of these heads significantly impacts task performance. Especially, we identify two classes of heads whose activations represent the abstract notion of true and false in GAR tasks respectively. They play fundamental roles in CRR across various models and tasks.

papers.title: BERTnesia: Investigating the capture and forgetting of knowledge in BERT
papers.research_question: The paper investigates how factual knowledge is stored across layers in BERT and how fine-tuning affects this knowledge.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that a significant amount of factual knowledge in BERT is stored in intermediate layers, not just the final layer, and that fine-tuning leads to forgetting of this knowledge, with the extent depending on the task and data.
papers.conclusion: Understanding how knowledge is stored and forgotten can help design better knowledge-intensive models and retrieval strategies.
papers.key_findings:
Intermediate layers of BERT contain a substantial amount of factual knowledge (17-60% across probes).
Knowledge evolves through layers, with some relation types best captured in intermediate layers.
Fine-tuning causes forgetting of relational knowledge, with ranking models forgetting the least and QA models the most.
Masked language modeling is more effective at acquiring new knowledge from fine-tuning data than QA or ranking.
The density of factual information in the training data affects knowledge retention.
papers.limitation: The probing task (masked language modeling) is the same as BERT's pre-training task, so good performance in the last layers might be partially attributed to task-based knowledge.
future_direction: Further research into understanding the parametric memory of language models.
Investigating the effect of training objectives on factual knowledge.
Designing novel retrieval strategies for extracting factual knowledge from BERT's parametric memory.
papers.abstract: Probing complex language models has recently revealed several insights into linguistic and semantic patterns found in the learned representations. In this article, we probe BERT specifically to understand and measure the relational knowledge it captures in its parametric memory. While probing for linguistic understanding is commonly applied to all layers of BERT as well as fine-tuned models, this has not been done for factual knowledge. We utilize existing knowledge base completion tasks (LAMA) to probe every layer of pre-trained as well as fine-tuned BERT models(ranking, question answering, NER). Our findings show that knowledge is not just contained in BERT's final layers. Intermediate layers contribute a significant amount (17-60%) to the total knowledge found. Probing intermediate layers also reveals how different types of knowledge emerge at varying rates. When BERT is fine-tuned, relational knowledge is forgotten. The extent of forgetting is impacted by the fine-tuning objective and the training data. We found that ranking models forget the least and retain more knowledge in their final layer compared to masked language modeling and question-answering. However, masked language modeling performed the best at acquiring new knowledge from the training data. When it comes to learning facts, we found that capacity and fact density are key factors. We hope this initial work will spur further research into understanding the parametric memory of language models and the effect of training objectives on factual knowledge. The code to repeat the experiments is publicly available on GitHub.

papers.title: Conceptual structure coheres in human cognition but not in large language models
papers.research_question: Does conceptual structure in large language models cohere across different probing tasks as it does in humans, or do human and LLM conceptual representations differ in robustness?
papers.core_contribution: Human conceptual structure is robust across different tasks and cultures, but large language models exhibit less coherence in conceptual structure across different probing tasks, indicating a lack of a stable conceptual core.
papers.conclusion: Human conceptual structure is robust to differences in task, language, and culture, while contemporary LLMs lack such coherence, highlighting a fundamental difference between human cognition and current machine language models.
papers.key_findings:
Human conceptual structure estimates from three different tasks (feature listing, triadic comparisons, pairwise ratings) are highly coherent (squared Procrustes correlations between 0.72 and 0.96).
LLM conceptual structure estimates vary depending on the probing task; for GPT-3, the squared Procrustes correlations between different task embeddings are lower (e.g., 0.72 between feature listing and triplet, 0.47 between feature listing and pairwise, 0.25 between triplet and pairwise).
LLM conceptual structure from verified feature lists aligns moderately well with human feature norms (squared Procrustes correlation 0.89), but other LLM-derived embeddings align less well.
Chain-of-thought prompting improves alignment with human conceptual structure for some models but does not achieve human-level coherence.
Embeddings from internal representations (e.g., GPT-3 hidden layers, word2vec, CLIP) do not cohere well with each other or with human embeddings.
papers.limitation:
The study uses a constrained set of 30 concepts from two domains; a larger scale study might reveal different results.
The LLM simulations did not employ advanced prompting techniques like tree-of-thought or self-consistency, which might improve coherence.
LLMs lack multimodal sensory experience that humans have, which might affect conceptual organization.
future_direction: Conduct a larger scale study on larger concept sets.
Investigate the use of advanced prompting techniques (e.g., tree-of-thought, self-consistency) to improve conceptual coherence in LLMs.
papers.abstract: Neural network models of language have long been used as a tool for developing hypotheses about conceptual representation in the mind and brain. For many years, such use involved extracting vector-space representations of words and using distances among these to predict or understand human behavior in various semantic tasks. Contemporary large language models (LLMs), however, make it possible to interrogate the latent structure of conceptual representations using experimental methods nearly identical to those commonly used with human participants. The current work utilizes three common techniques borrowed from cognitive psychology to estimate and compare the structure of concepts in humans and a suite of LLMs. In humans, we show that conceptual structure is robust to differences in culture, language, and method of estimation. Structures estimated from LLM behavior, while individually fairly consistent with those estimated from human behavior, vary much more depending upon the particular task used to generate responses--across tasks, estimates of conceptual structure from the very same model cohere less with one another than do human structure estimates. These results highlight an important difference between contemporary LLMs and human cognition, with implications for understanding some fundamental limitations of contemporary machine language.

papers.title: A Glitch in the Matrix? Locating and Detecting Language Model Grounding with Fakepedia
papers.research_question: What are the mechanisms underlying LLMs' ability to ground answers in contextual information that contradicts their parametric knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Fakepedia, a counterfactual dataset, and MGCT, a causal mediation analysis method, to study grounding in LLMs, finding that grounding is a distributed process and that computational patterns can predict grounding behavior.
papers.conclusion: The findings show that grounding is a distributed process, ungrounded responses involve factual recall in MLPs, and grounding can be predicted from computation patterns, contributing to a coherent narrative of grounding and factual recall mechanisms.
papers.key_findings:
Grounding, contrary to factual recall, is a distributed process without clear localization.
The activity of a few MLPs differs significantly between grounded and ungrounded modes.
Computational patterns can predict whether a model is grounded with 92.8% accuracy.
Models exhibit diverse grounding behaviors; e.g., Mistral-7B is highly compliant while GPT-4 Turbo strongly prefers parametric knowledge.
Not grounding involves activating factual recall processes in the MLPs of the final subject token.
papers.limitation:
Descriptive analysis may be influenced by the choice of prompting strategy.
Mediation setup requires the object token to be the last token; different behaviors might emerge in other setups.
Automatic detection model may not generalize outside the experimental domain.
Does not distinguish between plausible and absurd counterfactual facts.
Dataset generation could be improved with interaction flows based on other language models as critics.
future_direction: Explore relationship between prompting strategy and grounding frequency.
Study grounding behavior in different experimental setups.
Investigate how grounding varies with the likelihood of counterfactual facts.
Improve dataset generation using language models as critics.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have an impressive ability to draw on novel information supplied in their context. Yet the mechanisms underlying this contextual grounding remain unknown, especially in situations where contextual information contradicts factual knowledge stored in the parameters, which LLMs also excel at recalling. Favoring the contextual information is critical for retrieval-augmented generation methods, which enrich the context with up-to-date information, hoping that grounding can rectify outdated or noisy stored knowledge. We present a novel method to study grounding abilities using Fakepedia, a novel dataset of counterfactual texts constructed to clash with a model's internal parametric knowledge. In this study, we introduce Fakepedia, a counterfactual dataset designed to evaluate grounding abilities when the internal parametric knowledge clashes with the contextual information. We benchmark various LLMs with Fakepedia and conduct a causal mediation analysis of LLM components when answering Fakepedia queries, based on our Masked Grouped Causal Tracing (MGCT) method. Through this analysis, we identify distinct computational patterns between grounded and ungrounded responses. We finally demonstrate that distinguishing grounded from ungrounded responses is achievable through computational analysis alone. Our results, together with existing findings about factual recall mechanisms, provide a coherent narrative of how grounding and factual recall mechanisms interact within LLMs.

papers.title: Co-occurrence is not Factual Association in Language Models
papers.research_question: Why do language models struggle to learn novel factual knowledge effectively from finetuning on limited textual demonstrations? Is it because they learn word co-occurrence statistics instead of true factual associations?
papers.core_contribution: Language models are biased to learn word co-occurrence statistics instead of true factual associations. We propose two strategies to improve learning of factual associations: using text with implicit associations and active forgetting.
papers.conclusion: Language models are biased to learn co-occurrence statistics, which hinders learning of generalizable factual knowledge. Using implicit association text and active forgetting can improve learning of factual associations.
papers.key_findings:
Co-occurrence statistics are easily learned from text with explicit co-occurrence, while factual associations are more easily learned from text with implicit association.
Knowledge in the form of co-occurrence statistics does not generalize well beyond simple QA, while factual associations generalize well to reasoning tasks.
Co-occurrence statistics and factual associations are parameterized in different layers: co-occurrence in middle layers, factual associations in lower layers.
Training on text with implicit association improves generalization of learned knowledge.
Active forgetting (resetting upper layer parameters) unblocks learning of factual associations and improves generalization.
papers.limitation:
Variation in forms of text: only two forms of text expressing factual knowledge are considered.
Methods for text generation: turning general text into text with implicit association may require complex rewriting.
The study is limited to finetuning of pretrained models, not pretraining from scratch.
Relationship to knowledge editing, knowledge-aware training and assisted reasoning: the study focuses on learning from raw text without annotations or reasoning assistance.
future_direction: Expand the investigation of knowledge learning efficiency to the pretraining phase.
Explore scalable data generation methods for efficient knowledge learning.
papers.abstract: Pretrained language models can encode a large amount of knowledge and utilize it for various reasoning tasks, yet they can still struggle to learn novel factual knowledge effectively from finetuning on limited textual demonstrations. In this work, we show that the reason for this deficiency is that language models are biased to learn word co-occurrence statistics instead of true factual associations. We identify the differences between two forms of knowledge representation in language models: knowledge in the form of co-occurrence statistics is encoded in the middle layers of the transformer model and does not generalize well to reasoning scenarios beyond simple question answering, while true factual associations are encoded in the lower layers and can be freely utilized in various reasoning tasks. Based on these observations, we propose two strategies to improve the learning of factual associations in language models. We show that training on text with implicit rather than explicit factual associations can force the model to learn factual associations instead of co-occurrence statistics, significantly improving the generalization of newly learned knowledge. We also propose a simple training method to actively forget the learned co-occurrence statistics, which unblocks and enhances the learning of factual associations when training on plain narrative text. On both synthetic and real-world corpora, the two proposed strategies improve the generalization of the knowledge learned during finetuning to reasoning scenarios such as indirect and multi-hop question answering.

papers.title: Mass-Editing Memory with Attention in Transformers: A cross-lingual exploration of knowledge
papers.research_question: This study examines the effectiveness of existing knowledge editing methods across languages and investigates the role of attention mechanisms in this process.
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes MEMAT, a knowledge editing method that modifies attention heads in addition to MLP layers, leading to improved performance, cross-lingual portability, and enhanced model understanding of edited facts.
papers.conclusion: MEMAT improves knowledge editing by leveraging attention heads, demonstrating portability and effectiveness across languages, and enhancing the model's understanding of the inserted factual associations.
papers.key_findings:
MEMIT's cross-lingual performance is dependent on subject tokenization similarity between languages.
Attention heads encode language-independent information about factual associations, achieving high accuracy in classifying truthful sentences.
MEMAT outperforms MEMIT across all evaluation metrics (success and magnitude), with improvements exceeding 10% in some cases.
The attention head corrections learned by MEMAT are portable and can be recycled for editing new sets of factual triplets.
MEMAT enhances the model's comprehension of the edited knowledge rather than merely reintroducing it, as evidenced by improved paraphrase and neighborhood metrics.
papers.limitation:
Experiments are limited to English and Catalan; generalization to other linguistic contexts may be limited due to alphabet similarity.
Broader challenges in knowledge editing persist, such as the inability to modify related knowledge and lack of bidirectionality.
future_direction: Investigating language adaptation techniques to enable models to perform tasks in a more language-agnostic manner.
Exploring the role that each architecture component plays in alternative domains to enhance explainable AI.
papers.abstract: Recent research has explored methods for updating and modifying factual knowledge in large language models, often focusing on specific multi-layer perceptron blocks. This study expands on this work by examining the effectiveness of existing knowledge editing methods across languages and delving into the role of attention mechanisms in this process. Drawing from the insights gained, we propose Mass-Editing Memory with Attention in Transformers (MEMAT), a method that achieves significant improvements in all metrics while requiring minimal parameter modifications. MEMAT delivers a remarkable 10% increase in magnitude metrics, benefits languages not included in the training data and also demonstrates a high degree of portability. Our code and data are at https://github.com/dtamayo-nlp/MEMAT.

papers.title: Generalisation First, Memorisation Second? Memorisation Localisation for Natural Language Classification Tasks
papers.research_question: In which layers of neural models does memorisation occur for natural language classification tasks?
papers.core_contribution: Memorisation is a gradual process across layers, task-dependent, and early layers are more important for memorisation in tasks where the model generalizes less well.
papers.conclusion: Memorisation is a gradual, task-dependent process, and early intervention is more successful for preventing memorisation.
papers.key_findings:
Memorisation is not confined to individual layers but is a cooperative process across many layers.
Early layers are generally more important for memorisation than later layers.
The depth of memorisation is task-dependent.
The better a model generalizes on a task, the more later layers are involved in memorisation.
Layer swapping and retraining are more reliable localisation techniques than gradients and probing.
papers.limitation:
Simplified data: label flipping to create noisy examples may not reflect real-world memorisation.
Limited to classification tasks, not generation or other NLP tasks.
Only 12-layer models were used in the main experiments, though Appendix B includes a 24-layer model.
Potential confounding factors such as label set size and task difficulty.
future_direction: Understanding what properties of a task direct memorisation to lower or higher layers.
Implications for model editing and safety.
papers.abstract: Memorisation is a natural part of learning from real-world data: neural models pick up on atypical input-output combinations and store those training examples in their parameter space. That this happens is well-known, but how and where are questions that remain largely unanswered. Given a multi-layered neural model, where does memorisation occur in the millions of parameters? Related work reports conflicting findings: a dominant hypothesis based on image classification is that lower layers learn generalisable features and that deeper layers specialise and memorise. Work from NLP suggests this does not apply to language models, but has been mainly focused on memorisation of facts. We expand the scope of the localisation question to 12 natural language classification tasks and apply 4 memorisation localisation techniques. Our results indicate that memorisation is a gradual process rather than a localised one, establish that memorisation is task-dependent, and give nuance to the generalisation first, memorisation second hypothesis.

papers.title: Does Time Have Its Place? Temporal Heads: Where Language Models Recall Time-specific Information
papers.research_question: How do language models internally handle and recall temporally changing facts? Specifically, where within the model architecture does the mechanism for time-specific knowledge reside?
papers.core_contribution: The paper discovers Temporal Heads, specific attention heads that mediate the recall of time-specific knowledge in LLMs. Ablating these heads degrades temporal fact recall while leaving time-invariant knowledge and general QA performance unaffected, and their activations can be used for temporal knowledge editing.
papers.conclusion: The work systematically uncovers Temporal Heads that selectively mediate time-variant knowledge in LLMs. These heads are causally important for temporal recall, can be activated by both numeric and textual time references, and offer a target for precise temporal knowledge editing without global retraining.
papers.key_findings:
Specific attention heads (Temporal Heads) are identified across multiple models (e.g., a15.h0, a18.h3 in Llama2) that are crucial for recalling time-specific facts.
Ablating Temporal Heads significantly reduces accuracy on temporal knowledge tasks but has minimal impact on time-invariant knowledge and general QA performance.
Temporal Heads are activated not only by numeric time conditions (e.g., 'In 2004') but also by textual aliases (e.g., 'In the year the Summer Olympics were held in Athens'), indicating they encode a broader temporal dimension.
The importance of Temporal Heads varies across different years and knowledge categories, with stronger effects around periods of factual transition.
Temporal knowledge can be edited by selectively adjusting the activation values of these heads, demonstrating their role as a key component for modifying time-sensitive information.
papers.limitation:
Analysis of unstructured temporal QAs like General ChroKnowledge was constrained, as the underlying multiple-choice options typically do not exhibit temporal dependencies.
The circuit analysis method (EAP-IG) did not support models with Grouped-Query Attention (GQA), excluding models like Llama-3-8B-Instruct from the main analysis.
future_direction: Future work should include broader application of the findings for enhancing temporal reasoning to increase practical value.

papers.title: Mass-Editing Memory in a Transformer
papers.research_question: How many memories can we add to a deep network by directly editing its weights? The paper investigates scaling up memory editing to thousands of associations in language models.
papers.core_contribution: MEMIT is a method for directly updating a language model with many memories by editing MLP weights in a range of critical layers, scaling to thousands of associations while maintaining generalization, specificity, and fluency.
papers.conclusion: MEMIT enables large-scale memory editing in transformers, and interpretability-based methods may become a practical alternative to opaque fine-tuning for editing, controlling, and auditing models.
papers.key_findings:
MEMIT scales to 10,000 edits on GPT-J and GPT-NeoX, exceeding prior work by orders of magnitude.
MEMIT outperforms fine-tuning, MEND, and ROME baselines on efficacy, generalization, and specificity metrics.
MEMIT maintains fluency and consistency of generations after mass edits.
MEMIT performs well across different categories of facts and when editing mixed sets of memories.
Certain relations (e.g., 'plays sport') are harder to edit with robust specificity, but MEMIT still outperforms other methods.
papers.limitation: The method is limited to directional (subject, relation, object) associations and does not cover symmetric relations, spatial/temporal reasoning, mathematical knowledge, or procedural knowledge.
papers.abstract: Recent work has shown exciting promise in updating large language models with new memories, so as to replace obsolete information or add specialized knowledge. However, this line of work is predominantly limited to updating single associations. We develop MEMIT, a method for directly updating a language model with many memories, demonstrating experimentally that it can scale up to thousands of associations for GPT-J (6B) and GPT-NeoX (20B), exceeding prior work by orders of magnitude. Our code and data are at https://memit.baulab.info.

papers.title: Are formal and functional linguistic mechanisms dissociated in language models?
papers.research_question: Do current large language models exhibit distinct localization (dissociation) of formal and functional linguistic mechanisms in their internal circuits?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds evidence for formal-functional dissociation in LLMs in terms of cross-task faithfulness (formal task circuits perform other formal tasks better than functional ones, and vice-versa), but not in terms of circuit overlap, suggesting a shared pool of mechanisms for formal tasks rather than a single unified region.
papers.conclusion: There is evidence for emerging formal-functional dissociation in LLMs in terms of cross-task faithfulness, but not in terms of circuit overlap, indicating a set of shared formal linguistic mechanisms rather than a single unified region.
papers.key_findings:
Circuits for formal and functional linguistic tasks have low overlap (IoU).
Circuits for formal tasks do not have especially high overlap with each other, arguing against a single unified formal network.
Formal task circuits perform other formal tasks better than they perform functional tasks (cross-task faithfulness).
Functional task circuits perform other functional tasks better than they perform formal tasks (cross-task faithfulness).
